patterns.name: Phased Refactoring for scope=all
patterns.description: Break large-scale refactoring into discrete functional phases with validation checkpoints. Each phase maintains system stability and allows incremental rollback.
patterns.approach:
1. Analyze codebase for refactoring opportunities
2. Create phase breakdown strategy (layer-based, component-based, complexity-based, or dependency-based)
3. Execute each phase with: checkpoint commit → plan approval → execute → validate → phase commit
4. Mandatory zero-tolerance validation between phases (0 errors, 0 warnings)
5. Independent rollback capability per phase
6. Final cross-phase validation and documentation
risks: Test code may have custom implementations not suitable for extraction
Previous refactorings may have already addressed opportunities
mitigations: Verify before extracting - check if patterns are truly identical
Review git history and checkpoint.json for completed refactorings
Start with low-risk phases (documentation, comments) before structural changes
Skip phases where previous work is sufficient

implementation_notes.phase_1_low_risk: Documentation cleanup, TODO marker updates, XML documentation - minimal risk
implementation_notes.phase_2_test_consolidation: Test helper extraction - RISK: Custom implementations may not be compatible
implementation_notes.phase_3_service_layer: Service consolidation - Check if already done (e.g., HtmlTransformPatterns.cs)
implementation_notes.phase_4_debug_infrastructure: Verify debug markers standardization - may already be complete
implementation_notes.phase_5_documentation: Final integration and learning pattern updates

patterns.name: Unified Service Wrapper Pattern
patterns.description: Create unified service wrapper that provides mode-based functionality while maintaining backward compatibility with existing services. Useful when multiple services have overlapping responsibilities but different contexts require different feature sets.
patterns.approach:
1. Identify services with overlapping responsibilities
2. Create wrapper service injecting existing services
3. Implement mode-based methods (e.g., TransformForHost vs TransformForParticipant)
4. Preserve original services for backward compatibility
5. Update consumers to use unified service where appropriate
6. Document architectural decisions and usage patterns
risks: Over-abstraction can make code harder to understand
Wrapper adds indirection layer (slight performance cost)
Components may still need direct service access for specific features
Inconsistent adoption if some components use wrapper, others use direct services
mitigations: Document when to use wrapper vs direct service access
Keep wrapper thin (delegate to existing services, don't reimplement)
Maintain clear mode separation (explicit method names)
Update all new components to use wrapper for consistency
Provide migration guide for existing components

implementation_notes.mode_separation: Host mode gets full features (transformation + share buttons), Participant mode gets safe rendering only
implementation_notes.backward_compatibility: Original services (HtmlParsingService, AssetProcessingService) remain available for components needing direct access
implementation_notes.error_handling: Unified service provides consistent error messages via CreateErrorMessage() helper
implementation_notes.type_conversion: Handle type conversions in wrapper (e.g., long sessionId → string runId)

code_example.consumer_usage:
private readonly UnifiedHtmlTransformService _transform;

var html = await _transform.TransformForHostAsync(rawHtml, sessionId);
